newsitem.title: FRANCE: French MPs debate controversial anti-poverty bill.
newsitem.headline: French MPs debate controversial anti-poverty bill.

text.p: France's National Assembly on Tuesday begins a marathon debate on a controversial anti-poverty bill aimed at delivering on President Jacques Chirac's 1995 campaign promises to heal the "social fracture" between rich and poor.

The package of measures, which would cost an estimated 2.5 billion francs ($431 million), is intended to boost the government's flagging popularity in the face of its inability to remedy record-high 12.8 percent unemployment.

The proposed legislation calls for the creation of 300,000 minimum-wage jobs over five years, the construction of 100,000 subsidised housing units and requisitioning vacant dwellings to house the homeless, and better access to health care for the needy.
But the opposition Socialists and private associations -- who estimate more than five million people in France live in poverty -- have lambasted the measures as not going far enough to help the poor.

"This is a bill of social incoherence because it takes from the poor to give to the poorer," said Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande. "It is absolutely necessary for this legislation to be changed, and for the most well-off to be giving to the poor."
More than 600 amendments to the legislation were put forward before the parliamentary session opened, many by members of the ruling conservative coalition.
The Socialists have said they would try to have the bill sent back to the parliament's Social Affairs Committee for improvements, a typical ploy to delay the vote.

The legislation, which would also reform the way government housing is distributed to give priority to the most needy, and encourage the homeless to register at social services agencies to gain the right to vote, will almost certainly be adopted given the government's overwhelming four-fifths majority.
Anti-poverty associations said the measures would for the most part be financed by funds skimmed from a new lower ceiling on welfare benefits.

"This is a law that has no other budget than that taken essentially from other welfare allocations, in other words money seized from the unemployed," said Laurent Guilloteau of the Act against Unemployment association.
The debate, initially expected to continue until late Thursday, is now planned to run into the beginning of next week to allow time to review the proposed amendments.
The Senate, France's upper house, is due to open debate on the bill in May.
